summary:
Bahrain decriminalised same-sex sexual activity in 1976, repealing a British colonial-era statute, and is the only Gulf state that does not explicitly penalise same-sex intimacy. No statute criminalises transgender expression. Guidance published by the United States Department of State records that arrests for homosexual behaviour are relatively rare.

Decriminalisation has not removed exposure. Articles 324, 329 and 350 of the penal code, covering indecency and debauchery, carry three months to two years' imprisonment, fines of up to 200 Bahraini dinars and deportation for non-Bahrainis. Authorities have applied them to people suspected of being LGBTQI+ or of cross-dressing: a man received a one-month sentence in 2009 for wearing an abaya and carrying a purse in public, police raided a 2011 party described as a same-sex wedding, and nine cross-dressers were arrested at a hotel discotheque party in Manama on New Year's Eve and charged with public debauchery. In February 2024 the Council of Representatives adopted further moral legislation, extending the framework under which such charges are brought.

Entry is an active screening point. The Interior Minister has stated that suspected effeminate homosexuals are barred from entering Bahrain through airport checks, and pending bills have proposed expressly banning LGBTQ foreigners from entry or from receiving residency permits. In September 2013 the Gulf Cooperation Council agreed to discuss a proposal to establish testing to exclude gay foreigners, though officials later backtracked.

Legal gender recognition is refused by the courts. In a May 2023 judgment a lower court rejected a trans man's application for legal gender recognition and gender-affirming healthcare, citing Islamic Sharia, and declined the Ministry of Health medical-committee examination he requested. A 2023 ruling held that sex-reassignment procedures are against Islamic law where a case is considered solely related to gender dysphoria, which confines eligibility to people with intersex traits. Courts require medical documentation of a sex-change operation or of medical necessity before a legal gender marker can be changed, and gender-affirming medical care is heavily restricted on that basis.

Article 330 of the penal code mandates that anyone charged with prostitution or fujoor be taken to a hospital for sexually transmitted disease testing and potentially relocated to a medical facility.

Bahrain has no legal protection against discrimination on the basis of sexual orientation, gender identity or expression, or sex characteristics, and no hate-crime framework covers LGBTQ people. Article 309 protects religious groups but does not extend equivalent protection to LGBTQ people, and hate speech against the community remains widespread with no legal consequences.

No LGBTQ-specific facilities, shelters or community organisations exist. The United States Department of State reports that there are no approved LGBTQ-related organisations, and ILGA concludes that it is improbable that any sexual- or gender-diversity group would be registered, because the body controlling association registration may refuse any group judged contrary to morality or public order. Under the 1976 penal code the age of adulthood for consensual same-sex acts is 21.
tangentialFactors:
Bahrain's decriminalisation sets it apart from every neighbouring Gulf jurisdiction, but the gap between statute and practice is where exposure sits: the morality and indecency provisions, not a sodomy offence, produce the arrests documented since 2009.

Youth are an explicit policy target. A bill proposed in October 2021 would have criminalised promoting or inviting others to homosexual gatherings with up to five years' imprisonment, and other pending bills proposed instructing teachers to spot warning signs of homosexuality or cross-dressing so that children could be punished.

Media hostility compounds official posture. On 3 August 2024 the newspaper Albilad published a widely viewed caricature depicting a pride-flag roll of toilet paper captioned 'the correct place'.
localsOnly:
False accusations of homosexuality are used as a tool to discredit and bully government critics and protesters, including human-rights advocate Nabeel Rajab and demonstrators at Pearl Roundabout in 2011.

The Education Ministry disclaims responsibility for sexuality issues. Responding to parliamentary questions about lesbianism in schools, Assistant Under-Secretary for Educational Services Khalid Al Alawi stated that the matter is parents' job and that 'The public shouldn't make a big deal out of this problem because it does not exist', while adding that students whose appearance is contrary to school values should be disciplined.

On 14 February 2024 the Ministry of Education referred a private school's administration and board to investigation and dismissed its general manager after a video showed students performing a scene with two male students pretending to propose to each other. A 2022 incident, in which a private school distributed material perceived as promoting homosexuality, also triggered calls for stricter laws.

Residents have no registered organisation to turn to: the body controlling association registration may refuse any group judged contrary to morality or public order, and no approved LGBTQ-related organisation exists.
outOfScopeNotes:
The Immigration and Refugee Board of Canada research response BHR105575.E of August 2016 reports that, according to sources including the Canadian government and Gulf News, homosexuality is illegal in Bahrain. That reading contradicts the 1976 decriminalisation recorded by Wikipedia, Outright International and the 2023 United States Department of State profile. The conflict is unresolved in the available sources.

Bahrain has denied entry to or impeded independent human-rights researchers for a decade, including United Nations human-rights bodies and Amnesty International, so local media often serve as the only source for this jurisdiction. Verification of enforcement practice is correspondingly thin.

The status of the pending bills on entry bans, youth promotion offences and school reporting is unresolved: the inventory records them as proposed or pending, not enacted, and does not source their current legislative fate.

Beyond the United States Department of State statement that arrests for homosexual behaviour are relatively rare, no source in the inventory quantifies how often the indecency provisions are applied, or records any enforcement against transgender people specifically.
